articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Iranian Shadow Banking Networks Under Operation Economic Outcast
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed sanctions on over two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel. This action, part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aims to disrupt Iran's global shadow banking networks.

The targeted entities are accused of facilitating billions of dollars in foreign currency transactions for Iran, circumventing comprehensive sanctions. The Treasury Department emphasized that these networks underpin much of Iran's remaining foreign trade.

The sanctions were imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, E.O. 13224, as amended, the United States' counterterrorism sanctions authority, and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in certain sectors of Iran's metals industry.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Oil Facilitators and Issues Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting previously designated entities. This action is part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' aimed at disrupting Iran's revenue sources.

Specifically, Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj were designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. They are described as part of a network recovering oil proceeds held in third countries.

Concurrently, OFAC issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions. FAQs 1277 and 1278 clarify that OFAC's sanctions authority covering Cuba's manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine sectors does not automatically sanction all persons operating in those sectors, and that authorized activities involving Cuba's marine sector, including payments to Cuban ports for authorized trade and certain humanitarian transactions, may continue.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Major Drug Trafficking Organizations and Cyber Scam Operators, Amends Russia GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced significant designations targeting international drug trafficking organizations and cyber-related scam networks. The Australia-based Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang and the Italy-based 'Ndrangheta mafia syndicate were sanctioned for their roles in global drug trafficking and money laundering, including activities benefiting terrorist cartels.

Additionally, OFAC sanctioned three individuals and two affiliated companies for operating or supporting Southeast Asia-based cyber scam centers that target Americans through virtual currency investment fraud. These actions were taken under Executive Order 13694, targeting scam compound operators and facilitators, including affiliates of armed groups providing protection and support to scam networks.

In a separate action, OFAC issued Illicit Drugs General License 1, authorizing the wind down of certain transactions involving persons blocked on November 19, 2026. Furthermore, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131L, authorizing certain transactions related to negotiating and entering into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with related maintenance activities, and amended associated Russia-related FAQs 1224 and 1225.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Embassy & Consulates in China

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new counter terrorism designations. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt and dismantle networks that support terrorist activities globally.
Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated and the nature of their support for terrorism were not immediately available in the initial announcement.
These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to utilizing its sanctions authorities to combat terrorism financing and related illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations Under Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Authorities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has imposed blocking sanctions against the Guatemala-based Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization under its narcotics and counterterrorism authorities. This action aims to disrupt the organization's illicit activities and its support for terrorism.

Additionally, OFAC added counterterrorism sanctions to the existing narcotics designation of the Los Huistas Drug Trafficking Organization. The State Department concurrently designated Los Lorenzanas as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and Specially Designated Global Terrorist.
These designations prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the blocked organizations unless authorized by a general or specific license issued by OFAC, or if an exemption applies.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has released an update regarding Iran-related designations. This update follows a series of recent actions targeting Iran's financial and petroleum sectors.

On November 6, OFAC designated eight Canada-based money services businesses for allegedly operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. These businesses are accused of exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, and many have dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the IRGC.

This action was coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's financial intelligence unit, and the Drug Enforcement Administration, highlighting international cooperation in combating illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-related Designations on Digital Asset Sector
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, specifically targeting entities operating in the digital asset sector. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's use of virtual currencies to circumvent sanctions.

Eight Canada-based money services businesses were designated for allegedly operating in the digital asset sector of the Iranian economy. These businesses are accused of exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets, with many having dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset addresses linked to the IRGC.

This move underscores the U.S. government's focus on emerging financial technologies and their potential exploitation by sanctioned regimes. The action was coordinated with FinCEN, Canada's financial intelligence unit, and the Drug Enforcement Administration.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Expands Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside significant expansions to Cuba sanctions. This action aims to disrupt illicit financial activities and further pressure the Cuban regime.

OFAC sanctioned five individuals and 41 entities allegedly linked to cyber-enabled fraud networks, most of them said to be supporting the previously sanctioned Prince Group Transnational Crime Organization. Additionally, Malaysian national Chui Kok Wa was designated for allegedly managing a scam network in Madagascar that targeted U.S. citizens.

On the same day, OFAC determined that the sector-based sanctions authority in Executive Order (E.O.) 14404 applies to the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy. This means any foreign person determined to operate, or have operated, in these sectors is now exposed to blocking sanctions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Customs & International Trade Law Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-related Entities, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing listings. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's illicit financial activities and its 'shadow fleet' operations.

Four individuals and nine entities allegedly linked to an India-based network supporting Iran's shadow fleet were sanctioned. OFAC also published an Iran-related alert concerning the Iranian Shadow Fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion.

Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) 5AA, which authorizes, on or after December 18, 2026, transactions related to, financing for, and other dealings in the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 percent bond that would otherwise be prohibited by subsection 1(a)(iii) of E.O. 13835, as amended. GL 5AA replaces and supersedes GL 5Z.

Parties engaging in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Remote Access to Advanced U.S. AI Technology
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued a new interim final rule to prevent foreign entities from circumventing U.S. export controls by remotely accessing advanced American computing technology through data centers located in third countries.

The rule, titled 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' establishes new licensing requirements for advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, servers, and certain overseas computing arrangements. It also introduces additional restrictions affecting exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

This interim final rule, effective November 19, 2026, formally rescinds the previous AI Diffusion Rule and imposes heightened due diligence requirements for semiconductor manufacturers to prevent the diversion of advanced chips to restricted end users.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities to Entity List Over Diversion Risk of Advanced Computing Commodities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List, under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This rule is effective November 23, 2026.

These entities, including Megaspeed International Pte and its owner Swiftdata, along with the Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix and Apex Enterprise Solutions (a Singapore subsidiary of Alibaba), have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

The additions are due to the significant risk of these entities being involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users. A license will now be required for all items subject to the EAR, with licenses reviewed under a presumption of denial.

articles.headline: TSMC and Samsung Halt Some China Chip Shipments Following New U.S. Export Rules
body: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers as they apply for U.S. export licenses. This action follows a new interim final rule from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) that took effect on November 19, 2026.

The new BIS rule narrows the ways a foundry can demonstrate that an advanced logic chip is outside U.S. controls, effectively removing a compliance route that allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licenses.

Affected customers are generally limited to older chipmaking technology, with orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometers and below now requiring U.S. export licenses. This move complicates Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives to advanced chips.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
